988.title: Family feuds
988.hook: old feuds cost more each year
988.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the quarrel of Miriam, Aaron and Moses in Numbers 12; the Talmud (Berakhot 34a) points to Moses's five-word prayer for his sister as an example of a short prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving strangers. Your line was they're having a day: pass it over, and remember you've had them too. Today, the opposite: people you can't stop seeing, because they're family.

A chair at the holiday table that nobody sits in anymore. A cousin who isn't invited, and nobody quite remembers why. Two sisters who send birthday messages through their mother. Family feuds have a way of outliving their reasons. The original argument fades, and what's left is the silence, which gets heavier as it ages: one more wedding missed, one more grandchild who's never met an aunt. A proverb has a picture for that weight, and the book of Numbers has a quarrel between three siblings, and the short sentence that began to end it.
screen: `THE EMPTY CHAIR.` → `THE REASON FADES. THE SILENCE STAYS.` → `THREE SIBLINGS, ONE QUARREL.`

segments.voice: First, why it gets harder. Proverbs eighteen says, in the King James words: "A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle." Every year of silence can feel like another bar across the gate. Second, the quarrel. In the book of Numbers, Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses, first about the woman he married, then about whether God speaks only through him. A family argument in the middle of the wilderness camp. Third, the step. In the story, Miriam is suddenly struck with leprosy, and Moses, the one spoken against, is the one who cries out for her: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." In Hebrew, the plea is five words long. No speech about who was right, no demand for an apology first. Just: let my sister be well. Fourth, who waits. Miriam has to stay outside the camp for seven days, and the text adds: "the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again." A whole people stays put until the sister is back inside. A family quarrel can hold everyone up, and the step that starts to end one can be as small as five words.
screen: `HARDER TO WIN THAN A STRONG CITY.` · `SPOKEN AGAINST BY HIS OWN.` · `HEAL HER NOW.` · `THE CAMP WAITS FOR MIRIAM.` · then, large: `ONE STEP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rift in your family, yours or one you're standing near, and don't try to solve it; just ask what the smallest possible step would be. Not a speech or a reunion, but something tiny: a like on a photo, a card, a neutral hello at the next gathering, or telling the people in someone else's quarrel that you'd rather stay out of it. Let a few options come, choose one and hold it lightly; you're only finding where the first stone is. If you pray, you can bring that family into your prayer.
Family feuds. Quarrels inside a family that outlive their reasons, and the small step that can begin to end them. Today's word.
Your line: one step. Five words began to bring Miriam back into the camp. See you tomorrow.

989.title: Your younger self
989.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including Psalm 25 with its request not to remember the sins of youth; Christians read Paul's line about childish things as part of his chapter on love, 1 Corinthians 13.

segments.voice: Yesterday, family feuds, and Moses praying five words for the sister who spoke against him. Your line was one step. Today, someone you've known longer than anyone: the person you used to be.

An old notebook turns up in a box during a move. The handwriting is yours, but the person writing isn't quite. There's the plan to marry someone who turned out to be a disaster. There's the cruel joke about a friend. There's the decision that cost a job, or a year, or a relationship. Some people laugh at their old notebooks; some close them fast. Earlier this block was about forgiving yourself in general. Today is narrower: the younger one, who had less to work with. Two lines from the Bible can be read as speaking to that person.
screen: `AN OLD NOTEBOOK.` → `YOUR HANDWRITING, NOT QUITE YOU.` → `THE YOUNGER ONE.`

segments.voice: First, a stage, not a verdict. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, says: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things." He doesn't say the child was wicked. He says the child understood as a child. The younger self had a smaller map, and acted inside it. Second, a prayer about youth. Psalm twenty-five asks: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD." Two rememberings: don't remember the sins; do remember me. The psalmist isn't asking to be excused. He's asking to be seen as more than the worst of his younger days. Third, the trick of hindsight. Looking back, the warning signs are obvious, because now you know how it ended. Your younger self didn't. Blaming them for not knowing the ending is like shouting at a character in a movie you've already seen. Fourth, what the line is not. I didn't know then isn't the same as it didn't matter. If someone was hurt, amends still apply: make it right where you can. Forgiving your younger self doesn't cancel the repair. It sets down the blame, so the person you are now has the energy to do the repairing.

Recall one thing that version of you did that still stings, then look at the person instead of the mistake: what did they know, what were they afraid of, who was teaching them? If it feels right, say your line silently to them, and if you pray, hold that younger self in your prayer.

Your line: I didn't know then. Hindsight knows the ending; they didn't. Day nine hundred eighty-nine, done.

990.title: Reconciling, when safe
990.hook: where it's safe, reconciliation is a gift to both
990.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 133, and its opening Hebrew words, hinneh mah tov, are sung as a song in many Jewish communities; readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter 79 as counsel on not pressing old claims after a quarrel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corinth, and your younger self. Your line was I didn't know then. Today, a step that takes two people, not one.

Two old friends pass in a grocery aisle. One hand goes halfway up, the other person nods, and both keep walking, carts rattling, each wondering if the other wanted to stop. A few weeks ago this path said forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship, and that's still true. But sometimes the distance isn't protecting anyone anymore. Sometimes the other person is safe, and sorry, or just as stuck. A Hebrew psalm and a Chinese classic each have a line about what happens when two people do stop.
screen: `A HALF-RAISED HAND.` → `FORGIVING CAN BE ALONE.` → `RECONCILING TAKES TWO.`

segments.voice: First, what it's for. Psalm 133 opens, in the King James words: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Not only right, but sweet to live in. The psalm compares it to fragrant oil running down Aaron's beard, and to dew falling on the mountains: things that run down and spread, reaching whatever they touch. Second, the honest catch. The Tao Te Ching, in chapter seventy-nine, says, in a paraphrase of James Legge's version, that when a great quarrel is settled, some resentment is sure to remain. Reconciling isn't a time machine. Two people who make up still remember. Third, what the wise one does with that. The same chapter pictures a tally, the old way of recording a debt in two halves, and says the sage keeps his half and doesn't press the other side to pay. One way to read it: reconciling isn't pretending there was no debt. It's holding the record without collecting on it. Fourth, the condition in your line. Reconciling is only a gift where it's safe. If the other person is still dangerous, still cruel, still doing the thing, the brave act may be the boundary from a few days ago, not the reunion. Nothing on this path asks anyone to walk back into harm. But where it is safe, a half-raised hand in a grocery aisle can be the start of something good and pleasant.
screen: `GOOD AND PLEASANT, TOGETHER.` · `SOME RESENTMENT REMAINS.` · `HOLD THE TALLY. DON'T COLLECT.` · `ONLY WHERE IT'S SAFE.` · then, large: `WHEN IT'S SAFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted from, where the drift is about time, pride or awkwardness, not danger. Ask yourself two questions: is it safe, and do I want this? If both answers are yes, find the simplest first sentence, short and true; if either is no, let them go back to the distance, and if you pray, you can bring them into your prayer.
Reconciling. Two people rebuilding what was broken between them: a step past forgiveness, taken only where it's safe. Today's word.
Your line: when it's safe. Where it isn't, the line is your permission to wait. Until tomorrow.

991.title: Letting the story change
991.hook: the story of the hurt can change as you do
991.howItsDone: Jews read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Christians read it among the books of the Old Testament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconciling, and the sage who keeps the tally without collecting. Your line was when it's safe. Today, something you can change even when no one else is willing: the way you tell it.

Every hurt comes with a story, and the story gets told. To a friend the week it happens, hot and fast. To a partner a year later, with a sigh. To yourself in the car, in the same words every time, like a song on repeat. The facts in those stories don't change; what happened, happened. But the telling can change, because the teller does. The book of Ruth has a woman whose story is told one way in its first chapter and another way in its last. Today: letting the story change.
screen: `EVERY HURT HAS A STORY.` → `THE FACTS STAY.` → `THE TELLER CHANGES.`

segments.voice: First, the first telling. Naomi has buried her husband and both her sons in a foreign country. When she comes home to Bethlehem, the women of the town ask, is this Naomi? She answers, in the King James words: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter. She renames herself after the hurt. Second, that telling was true. She goes on: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." The book doesn't correct her. Nobody tells her to look on the bright side. The bitter telling gets its full say, and it stays in the book. Third, the second telling. By the last chapter a lot has happened: Ruth's loyalty, a harvest, a marriage, a baby. And the women of the town tell the story again: "There is a son born to Naomi." Naomi, not Mara. The graves from chapter one are still there. What changed is that the story kept going, and so did she. Fourth, a test for a new telling. Is it still true? Does it still name the loss, or the wrong, plainly? And does it have room for who you are now, not only who you were the day it happened? A new telling isn't a happier lie. It's the same facts, told by someone who has kept living.
screen: `CALL ME MARA.` · `I WENT OUT FULL.` · `A SON BORN TO NAOMI.` · `THE SAME FACTS, A LIVING TELLER.` · then, large: `A NEW TELLING.`

segments.voice: Choose one hurt you've told many times, and hear the usual telling once, in its usual words. Now tell it again silently, keeping the facts exactly and naming the wrong plainly, but add one sentence about what came after, something you did, learned or survived; if there's no after yet, the sentence can be: and I'm still here. Let the new telling sit without forcing a happy ending, and if you pray, you can offer both versions in your prayer.
Mara. The name Naomi gave herself after her losses, bitter, before the story was told again at the book's end. Today's word.
Your line: a new telling. Naomi's story didn't stop at Mara. That's day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: Before sleep
992.hook: a traditional Jewish bedtime prayer begins by forgiving anyone who hurt you that day
992.howItsDone: Jews who say the bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al ha-Mitah) begin, in the traditional prayer book, with a passage forgiving anyone who wronged them, before saying the Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara, and Naomi's story told twice. Your line was a new telling. Today, a practice for the end of every day, before the stories pile up.

What does the mind do in the last minutes before sleep? Lights off, phone down, and the day starts replaying. The comment in the meeting. The text that was a little too short. The friend who didn't ask how it went. Small things, mostly. But small things left overnight have a way of being bigger by morning, and bigger still by the end of the week. A Jewish tradition has an answer built into bedtime itself. Before the Shema is said at night, a prayer comes first, and it opens with forgiveness.
screen: `LIGHTS OFF. THE DAY REPLAYS.` → `SMALL THINGS GROW OVERNIGHT.` → `A PRAYER AT THE BEDSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. The bedtime Shema is a set of prayers said at night, at home, often in bed. In the traditional prayer book, before the Shema itself, there's a short passage addressed to the Master of the world. Second, what it says. In paraphrase: I hereby forgive anyone who angered me or wronged me, whether against my body, my property or my honor, by accident or on purpose, in word or in deed. It doesn't ask who deserves it, and it isn't limited to today. It covers the whole list in one sweep. Third, the line that surprises people. The prayer goes further: it asks that no one be punished on my account. Not just I let it go, but I don't want them to suffer because of what they did to me. That's a big request to make about someone who was rude to you at lunch, and it's said at night, while the day's grudges are still fresh. Fourth, a neighbor. Christians read a line from the letter to the Ephesians that points at the same hour: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Two traditions, each in its own words, both asking that the day's anger be set down at the edge of night. Clear the small debts daily, the way you'd wash the dishes before bed, so you don't wake up to a sink full of them.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE THE SHEMA.` · `BODY, PROPERTY, HONOR.` · `LET NO ONE BE PUNISHED FOR ME.` · `NOT THE SUN ON YOUR WRATH.` · then, large: `I FORGIVE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Whatever the hour, sit as if it were the end of the day, and flip back through today, or yesterday if it's morning, like photos. At each small sting, a word, a look, a silence, don't argue the case; just say silently, I forgive today, and move to the next. If something is too big for tonight, set it aside, and if you pray, you can use a bedtime prayer from your own tradition.
Before sleep. The last minutes of the day, when a Jewish bedtime prayer forgives the day's wrongs before the Shema is said. Today's word.
Your line: I forgive today. Small debts, cleared before they pile up. Day nine hundred ninety-two, done.

993.title: Yom Kippur
993.hook: the Day of Atonement: Jews fast, pray and ask forgiveness
993.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur Jews fast from evening to evening and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer, including confession; in the days before it, people seek out those they've wronged to ask forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before sleep, and the bedtime prayer that forgives first. Your line was I forgive today. Today a new stretch begins: the holy days the traditions set aside for forgiveness. First, the Jewish one.

No breakfast. No lunch. No coffee. A whole community, from evening to evening, puts down food and drink and spends the day in prayer. And the subject of all those hours isn't a victory or a harvest. It's what went wrong this year, and how to set it right. Earlier on this path came the Days of Awe, the time for making amends. This is the day they end on. Its name, in Hebrew, is Yom Kippur. In English: the Day of Atonement.
screen: `NO FOOD. NO DRINK.` → `A WHOLE DAY OF PRAYER.` → `THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the text. Leviticus gives the day its purpose, in the King James words: "For on that day shall the priest make an atonement for you, to cleanse you, that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD." Clean. The day is a washing, not a punishment. Second, how it's kept. Leviticus also says: "there shall be a day of atonement: it shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall afflict your souls". Jewish tradition reads afflicting the soul as fasting and other kinds of going without. The body's ordinary comforts step aside so the attention can go somewhere else. Third, the order. Twice on this path, on days nine hundred forty-two and nine hundred seventy-eight, came the Mishnah's rule: the day atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between people, not until you've made peace with the person you wronged. So the real work of Yom Kippur often starts before it: phone calls, apologies, asking forgiveness face to face. Fourth, what it adds up to: a cleansing before God, a fast that clears the ordinary out of the way, and peace made with people first. The day isn't only about being sorry. It's about coming back into right relationship, with God, with each other, and with the person you mean to be.
screen: `TO CLEANSE YOU.` · `YE SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS.` · `MAKE PEACE WITH PEOPLE FIRST.` · `COMING BACK INTO RELATIONSHIP.` · then, large: `ATONEMENT.`

segments.voice: Ask one question and let it stay open: where did I miss the mark this year? Not where others did; where I did. Let one or two answers come without arguing, then ask a second: is there someone I need to speak to before anything else can be set right? If you pray, you can bring both answers into your prayer.
Yom Kippur. The Day of Atonement, when Jews fast, pray and ask forgiveness, of God and, first, of one another. Today's word.
Your line: atonement. A washing, not a punishment, and peace with people first. See you tomorrow.

994.title: Kshamavani, the Jain day
994.hook: at the end of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of all beings: micchami dukkadam
994.howItsDone: At the close of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of family, friends, neighbors and all living beings, in person, by letter or by message, with the words micchami dukkadam; the pratikramana rite includes a verse forgiving and asking forgiveness of all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Your line was atonement. This week ran from family feuds to your younger self, reconciling, a new telling, bedtime and the Day of Atonement. Today it closes with two words sent in every direction.

The same two words arrive from all over in one morning: a coworker's message, a cousin's post, a card from a neighbor. Micchami dukkadam. No context, no list of what went wrong, just the phrase, sent to people near and far. For Jains, it marks the day at the end of Paryushana, a season of fasting, study and self-examination. Jains call the closing day by more than one name; one of them is Kshamavani, the day of forgiveness. And the forgiveness asked for on that day doesn't stop at friends and family. It reaches every living thing.
screen: `TWO WORDS, MANY DIRECTIONS.` → `THE END OF PARYUSHANA.` → `EVERY LIVING THING.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Micchami dukkadam comes from Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures. Jains explain it as asking that whatever wrong I did be in vain, undone, without fruit. It's a request, not a speech; nobody has to name what happened. Second, the verse behind it. Jains recite a short verse in their rite of repentance, called pratikramana. In paraphrase: I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all, and enmity with none. It goes both ways in one breath: I forgive, and forgive me. Third, how wide it reaches. In Jain teaching, all living beings means exactly that: not only people, but animals, insects, the smallest creatures, the ones harmed without anyone noticing. That fits ahimsa, the Jain teaching of doing no harm. So the asking reaches a whole world someone has moved through all year, often carelessly. Fourth, why strangers too. The message goes out to people you may not have wronged at all, or don't remember wronging. That's the point. It doesn't wait for a complaint. It assumes that in a year of living, a person steps on more toes than they know, and it clears the ground anyway: two words, sent wide, asking to start the next season clean.
screen: `LET MY WRONG BE IN VAIN.` · `I FORGIVE, AND FORGIVE ME.` · `ALL LIVING BEINGS.` · `IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `MICCHAMI DUKKADAM.`

segments.voice: Start close, and hold in mind for a few breaths one person you know you've hurt this year. Then widen to people you may have hurt without knowing, a short reply, a missed call, someone you talked over, and wider still, to the creatures whose homes your life touches, until the circle is bigger than you can see. If it fits for you, silently offer the Jain phrase, micchami dukkadam, to the whole circle, or, if you pray, do this in your prayer.
Kshamavani. The Jain day of forgiveness at the close of Paryushana, when people ask pardon of all living beings. Today's word.
Your line: micchami dukkadam. No list needed, and no one left out. Day nine hundred ninety-four, done.
